title: What clients pay lobbyists
question: Who pays to lobby City Hall, how much, and how has the total moved since 2010?
finding: Lobbyists reported $173.3 million from 2,520 clients between January 2010 and October 2026: $6.0 million in 2010, a high of $13.7 million in 2019 and $12.7 million in 2025. The ten largest clients account for 12.4%; the largest are Prologis ($2.7 million), Recology ($2.5 million), Golden State Warriors ($2.5 million). Separately, 22 organizations that registered because they spend on campaigns to sway City decisions reported $3.3 million of such spending since 2019, led by Juul Labs, Inc. ($780,646), Mission for All, LLC ($756,446).
how: Every entry of the kind the lobbyist reports call “PaymentReceived” (a payment from a client, by month) is summed by client. Where two lobbyists at one firm report the same client, date and amount, it is counted once. Client names are grouped after removing punctuation and company suffixes. City payments are the Controller’s totals for the same name, fiscal 2019 to 2026. The year 2026 runs to October.
limits: Lobbying is registered, and so is giving by a lobbyist’s clients and colleagues. The figures are what lobbyists themselves filed; nobody audits them against the firms’ books, and a retainer can cover work other than lobbying. A company that lobbies with its own employees reports their pay as a payment from itself, shown here as “its own staff”. The number of payment entries went from 1,357 in 2013 to 3,673 in 2015 and 6,004 in 2017, far faster than the dollars, which points to fuller reporting of small clients rather than a tripling of lobbying; comparisons across those years should be read with that in mind. Name grouping can split one client filed under two different names.
